https://auto.economictimes.indiatimes.co.text: During a government news conference last week, Magyar said that as far as I know, an investigation had been launched concerning Szijjartos connections to the Russian government.Hungary's government announced an investigation Monday into a large foreign investment by Chinese automaker BYD negotiated by a former foreign minister who last week resigned from Parliament to take an executive position at the company.Peter Szijjarto's announcement last Wednesday that he would take the job at the world's top electric carmaker prompted accusations of a conflict of interest and criticism over his role in facilitating substantial government subsidies to the company while in office.Prime Minister Peter Magyar told lawmakers on Monday that Szijjarto, a close ally of former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, had helped BYD while he was in office "with hundreds of billions (of forints) in public money, diplomatic support and state infrastructure.""We will examine all the decisions, negotiations and state commitments made by Peter Szijjarto that were related to the BYD Hungary investment," Magyar said Monday.He added the investigation would look into all subsidies, tax breaks, permits, environmental exemptions and publicly-funded investments given to large multinational firms during Orban's tenure."We will investigate who made these decisions, who prepared them, what professional warnings were ignored, and how much burden they left on Hungarian taxpayers, workers, local communities and the environment," Magyar said.Neither Szijjarto nor BYD have responded to Magyar's allegations of conflict of interest while Szijjarto was in office. The former foreign minister has posed his new job as a "prestigious" opportunity to work for one the "greatest success stories" in the automotive industry.While serving in government, Szijjarto was instrumental in securing foreign investments in Hungary from Chinese companies, including his now-employer BYD, which received considerable state subsidies during his tenure.In 2023, Szijjarto announced that BYD would open its first European factory in Hungary - allowing the conglomerate to skirt European Union import tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles imposed to protect the continent's domestic auto manufacturing sector.In 2025, Szijjarto also announced BYD would locate its European headquarters and a research and development center in Budapest and receive 20 billion forints ($63.7 million) in government assistance.The investments were part of the Orban government's push to make Hungary a global hub of lithium-ion battery manufacturing, largely through attracting Chinese battery manufacturers who opened a series of plants across the country.The moves led local residents, environmentalists and opposition politicians to protest over fears the new industry would exacerbate existing environmental problems, hit the country's precious water supplies and further undermine its economy to China.While foreign minister, Szijjarto also maintained close relations with Russia despite its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022. Breaking with nearly all of his EU counterparts, he frequently traveled to Moscow to negotiate agreements on purchasing Russian oil and gas and to meet with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, whom he referred to as his "friend."He was embroiled in controversy during Hungary's 2026 election campaign when the Washington Post reported that he made regular phone calls to Lavrov during high-level EU meetings with "live reports on what's been discussed."Szijjarto has dismissed the report while acknowledging that he conferred with Lavrov before and after EU foreign minister meetings about their agenda and decisions.During a government news conference last week, Magyar said that "as far as I know," an investigation had been launched concerning Szijjarto's connections to the Russian government.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/09/08/saudi.text: Saudi Arabia hit back with a series of strikes on Tuesday after the Iran-backed Houthis targeted oil facilities and other sites across the border in their heaviest attack in years.The rapid exchange of fire follows the unravelling of a four-year truce in July, months into the war between the United States and Iran.Saudi strikes hit Taiz province, where deadly fighting has raged for days, and Marib province, the Houthis' Almasirah TV station said. There was no immediate comment from Riyadh.Overnight, Houthi attacks caused "temporary" shutdowns at oil sites and left 73 injured, authorities said. Saudi officials had vowed to respond.The latest strikes add to a rapidly deteriorating situation in Yemen, where hundreds have died in recent days as the Houthis try to capture land at the mouth of the Red Sea from the forces of the internationally-recognised government.The Houthis, who control about one-third of Yemen's territory — albeit the most densely populated parts — are vying to seize the narrow Bab al-Mandeb strait, an increasingly important route for oil after Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, slowing Gulf exports to a trickle.Houthi attacks on oil infrastructure and Saudi tankers have further contributed to a spike in oil prices, which leapt towards $100 a barrel on Tuesday.Houthis claim revengeThe group accused Riyadh on Monday of an attack on a prison that killed 11 people and left 20 inmates missing, according to the Houthi-controlled Almasirah TV channel.The Houthis said they fired dozens of ballistic missiles, hitting Abha International Airport, King Khalid air base and facilities belonging to Saudi state oil giant Aramco in Abha and Jizan.An energy ministry source told the Saudi Press Agency that "several energy sector facilities and installations" in the south were targeted."The attacks caused fires at several locations, leading to a temporary halt in some operations" as well as several injuries, the source said.Jizan, on the Red Sea coast just north of Saudi's Yemen border, has one of the country's biggest oil refineries with a capacity of 400,000 barrels per day.According to maritime tracking company Kpler, it was out of action for several weeks until at least 20 August following earlier Houthi attacks.Saudi Arabia's Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan said the door to diplomacy was still open, but Riyadh was ready to defend itself."The Kingdom will always support peace and diplomatic solutions," he said during a press conference in Moscow."However, (Saudi Arabia) will not hesitate to defend itself, protect its interests, and support measures that secure the interests, security, and stability of brotherly Yemen."'Spiral of escalation'The Houthis triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen's civil war in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace. Riyadh retaliated by striking the airport.The Saudi-led coalition, which has been fighting the Houthis on the internationally recognised government's behalf since 2015, said it would "take all necessary measures and actions to respond to the sources of the threat and neutralise its danger".Andreas Krieg, a Gulf expert from King's College London, said the Houthi attacks create an "extremely uncomfortable dilemma" for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto Saudi ruler.After years of trying to withdraw from the Yemen war, "restraint now carries the risk of allowing the Houthis to dictate the spiral of escalation," he said."Saudi Arabia's immediate response is likely to remain measured, involving airstrikes, intelligence support, and the reinforcement of Yemeni government forces," Krieg added."Should attacks on Saudi cities persist, maintaining this restraint will become increasingly difficult. In effect, the Houthis are testing exactly where Riyadh's true red line now lies."Formally known as Ansar Allah, the Houthis came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile.The group is part of Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.While the Houthis do not control the part of Yemen’s coastline along Bab el-Mandeb, they hold territory less than 100 kilometres away.The strait, whose name in Arabic means "Gate of Tears," connects the southern Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, and carries roughly 12% of global maritime trade.The Houthis disrupted it severely with their campaign against Israel-linked shipping during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, claiming it was a show of support for Palestinians.

https://telex.hu/eszkombajn/2026/09/26/u.text: Menü Kereső Ufóészlelésekre vezethető vissza a kolozsvári Hója-erdő paranormális turisztikai népszerűsége Észkombájn Transtelex Illusztráció: Dalmasso Monica / Hemis / AFP Tamás Zsófia (Transtelex) Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Misztikus eltűnések legendái és természetfeletti jelenlétről szóló beszámolók övezik a paranormális turizmus kedvelőinek egyik népszerű, kolozsvári úti célját, a Hója-erdőt. De hogyan lett a helyiek népszerű kirándulóhelyéből az ötvenes évek után a kísérteties helyek kedvelőinek látványossága, amely már-már a Drakula-kastély népszerűségével vetekszik? A Hója-erdő a maga 295 hektáros területével Kolozsvár nyugati részén található, a Törökvágás nevű hágón. A hely egy része Natura 2000-es természetvédelmi terület , népszerűsége azonban elsősorban nem a biodiverzitásának köszönhető. A tölgyfaerdőt még a BBC is a világ „legkísértettebb” helyei közé sorolta, a Guardian pedig hosszan cikkezett arról, hogy miért nevezik ezt a helyet az „erdélyi Bermuda-háromszögnek”. A lap riportere egy éjszakai vezetett sétán vett részt a Hója-erdőben, ahol saját bőrén tapasztalta meg az elmondása szerint hátborzongató helyszín adottságait. Elsőként Alexandru Sift biológus foglalkozott az ottani vélt paranormális jelenségek vizsgálatával, őt a helyiek fantasztikus történetei vonzották az erdőbe. Az ötvenes években rögzítette tapasztalatait kamerával, ezeken a felvételeken pedig megmagyarázhatatlan fény-árnyék jelenségeket, azonosíthatatlan és felismerhetetlen formákat észlelt. Halála után dokumentumarchívuma megsemmisült, a pár megmaradt fénykép azonban máig referenciapontként szolgál a paranormális jelenségek kedvelői körében. Az erdő 1968-ban került a nemzetközi figyelem középpontjába, amikor Emil Barnea katonai technikus elmondása szerint egy azonosítatlan repülő tárgyat fényképezett le, ahogy az elsuhant a fák felett , amikor ő épp a párjával sétált az erdőben. A képen egy elmosódott folt látható a fák felett, Barnea úgy írta le az Informația Bucureștiuluinak adott interjújában, mint egy „zajtalan, folyamatosan mozgásban lévő, fémes fényt árasztó objektum”, amihez hasonlót még sosem látott. A felvétel elindította az erdő iránti, azóta is fennálló nemzetközi érdeklődést. „Repülő tárgy Kolozsvár közelében, amelyet a fiatal Emil Barnea örökített meg” – A Romania Liberă 1968-as szeptemberi lapszáma Ami ezt a történetet megkülönbözteti más ufóészlelésektől, az az, hogy Barneának semmi haszna nem származott a történetből, veszítenivalója azonban volt bőven. A Romániában akkor fennálló szocialista rendszer ugyanis a paranormális jelenségekben való hitet nemcsak hogy őrültségnek titulálta, de gyakran államellenes szabotázsként is kezelte. Bár a kép nyilvánosságra került, és több sajtóorgánum is leközölte mint fantasztikumot, már akkor megosztotta a közvéleményt. Élénk vita bontakozott ki, Barneát és barátnőjét interjúkban szerepeltették az állami televízióban, sőt állítólag a titkosszolgálat emberei szenzoros hazugságvizsgálónak is alávetették őket, ami azonban nem bizonyította, hogy ne mondtak volna igazat. A tudományos körök szkeptikusan fogadták az esetet. A kolozsvári csillagvizsgáló igazgatója például azt állította, hogy a képek meteorológiai ballonokat ábrázolnak, vagy egyszerű csalásról van szó, miközben Barneát személyében is támadta, alkoholistának és írástudatlannak titulálva. Ugyanakkor több független szakértő – köztük fotósok, laboratóriumi elemzők és a Kolozsvári Egyetem technikusai – vizsgálta a negatívokat, és mindannyian arra a következtetésre jutottak, hogy semmilyen manipulációra utaló nyom nincs a képeken. A fény-árnyék viszonyok vizsgálata alapján azt is megállapították, hogy az objektum valószínűleg saját fényt bocsátott ki, nem csupán visszaverte a napfényt. Az 1977-es, első nemzetközi ufókonferencián, Acapulcóban be is mutatták Barnea képeit. Ebben a környezetben pedig már jóval pozitívabb volt a fotók fogadtatása , amelyeket akkor a világ legélesebb, legértelmezhetőbb ufófelvételei közé soroltak. Adrian Pătruț, a kolozsvári Babeș–Bolyai Egyetem vegyészprofesszora és egyben a Román Parapszichológiai Társaság elnöke 1995-ben kiadott, Fenomenele de la pădurea Hoia Baciu című könyvében tudományos hátterű, több évtizedes helyszíni kutatást mutat be a Hója-erdő rendhagyó jelenségeiről. A paranormális jelenségekről megállapítja, hogy véletlenszerűek, ezért statisztikai elemzésük nem lehetséges. Kimondja azt is, hogy bár egyes megnyilvánulások feltűnően hasonlítanak a hagyományosan ufóként emlegetett jelenségekre, általában nem mutatják az ufológiai fenomenológia specifikus és jellegzetes vonásait, legalábbis ami az erre vonatkozó szakirodalmi meghatározásokat illeti. „Rendkívül nehéz következtetést levonni. Az egyetlen biztos dolog, hogy ezek a jelenségek léteznek, és rendkívül egzotikus viselkedésük van, amelyet legalábbis jelenleg nem lehet az általánosan elfogadott tudományos paradigmákba sorolni” – fogalmazza meg a konklúzióját Pătruț. Az erdő mint turistalátványosság a BBC cikkében is megjelent, ahol úgy hivatkoznak a területre, mint amit az ott élők egyirányú átjáróként írnak le , ahova ha bemegy valaki, nem jön ki többet. „Azok, akik túlélték, azt mondják, hogy egész idő alatt rosszul érezték magukat és féltek. Azt mondják, a fák régen egyenesek és magasak voltak, mára már görbék és csavartak” – áll a cikkben. Az erdő valóban népszerű a paranormális jelenségekkel foglalkozók szubkultúrájában, több tartalomgyártó is tematizálta az azt övező legendákat és feltételezett természetfeletti jelenségeket. Podcastokban és videókban úgy emlegetik, mint portált egy másik dimenzióba vagy egyszerűen csak mint a legkísértettebb erdőt, de ott felszívódott gyerekekről, csoportokról is szó esik, és visszatérő elem a juhász legendája, akinek a juhaival együtt veszett ott nyoma. Egy több mint kétmilliós megtekintésű videóban szó esik olyan esetekről is, ahol az ufójelenéseket megörökítő felvételek egyszerűen eltűntek a készülékekről, amelyekkel rögzítették őket, de olyan emberek beszámolóit is említi, akiknek a kamerája látszólag ok nélkül merült le, ahogy beértek az erdőbe. Ha azonban az ember összeszedi a bátorságát és meglátogatja az erdőt, kevésbé fantasztikus és hátborzongató élményben lesz része, mint amit a YouTube-on beharangoznak neki, legalábbis a TripAdvisor és a Google Térkép értékelései ezt mutatják. „Elég fantasztikus, de közel sem olyan kísérteties, mint ahogy a »kísértetiességi« értékelések alapján gondolnám” – áll egy visszajelzésben. Többen is csalódottan írták, hogy nem találkoztak sem ufóval, sem szellemekkel az erdőben, de olyan is van, aki arra hívta fel a figyelmet, hogy az egyetlen dolog, amitől félni kell a Hójában, azok a kullancsok. Vannak azonban olyanok is, akik fura hangokról és kísérteties hangulatról számoltak be, sőt akad, aki elmondása szerint saját bőrén érezte a kísértetjárást. Az egyik felhasználó azt állította, hogy sötétedés után felébrednek a kísértetek az erdőben, amikor ott sátorozott, a sikolyok eléggé megnehezítették az elalvást éjszaka. Ezért értelemszerűen gyerekeknek nem ajánlja a látogatást. Az erdő egyik kiemelten „kísértett” része, ahol az eredeti ufófelvételek is készültek 1968-ban, a Kerek-tisztás (Poiana Rotundă), egy kopár rész az erdő közepén. Sokan már a létét és a formáját is természetellenes jelenségként definiálják, ugyanis a hozzá kapcsolódó történeteknek tulajdoníthatóan párhuzamot vélnek felfedezni az ufóleszállásokkal azonosított gabonakörökkel. Minderre azonban, ahogy a legtöbb ilyen jelenségre, van tudományos magyarázat: egy ökológiai jelenségről van szó, a talajösszetétel, a mikroklíma és a talajvízszint magyarázza a fák hiányát. A Hója-erdőben a Skeptoid elemzése szerint semmi bizonyíték nincs paranormális jelenségekre. A cikk szerzője kifejti, hogy a turisták által tapasztalt telefon- és kamerazavarok valószínűleg gyenge térerőből, akkumulátorhibákból vagy környezeti tényezőkből adódnak, nem „energiamező” okozza ezeket. A hely paranormális hírneve inkább a média, a helyi turizmus és a misztikus történetek által felerősített folklór, mintsem valós jelenségek következménye. Nincs dokumentált bizonyíték természetfeletti jelenlétre, minden állítólagos furcsaság magyarázható természetes, pszichológiai vagy környezeti okokkal. Az egyik legmeghatározóbb pszichológiai tényező a pareidolia, ami mindenkinek ismerős lehet egy horrorfilm megnézése után, ha maga a megnevezés idegennek hat is. Azt az állapotot írja le, amikor az emberi agy ismerős mintákat lát bele véletlenszerű formákba vagy zajokba, előzetes tudásra, ismeretekre és elvárásokra alapozva. Az ufóészlelés helyszíne, a Kerek-tisztás (Poiana Rotundă) – Forrás: Google Maps A Hója-erdő környezetvédelmi helyzete napjainkban rendezetlen és konfliktusos. Bár a kolozsvári civilek és szakértők évek óta kérik az egész terület védetté nyilvánítását, ez mindeddig nem történt meg, miközben az erdőt fakitermelés, ingatlanfejlesztések és közlekedési infrastruktúra is veszélyezteti. A legutóbbi vita egy kéthektáros tarvágás miatt robbant ki, amelyet a hatóságok jogszerű, előre tervezett erdőgazdálkodási munkaként írtak le, a civilek és a szakértők azonban megkérdőjelezték a szükségességét. A civilek továbbra is sürgetik a Hója védett területté nyilvánítását, a fakitermelés szigorúbb ellenőrzését, valamint azt, hogy a közelbe tervezett körgyűrű és az új építkezések ne veszélyeztessék tovább az erdő ökológiai és közösségi funkcióit. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Die Linke’s top candidate, Elif Eralp (with flowers) during a meeting of its Berlin state branch on 25 September 2026. Photograph: Tobias Schwarz/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Die Linke’s top candidate, Elif Eralp (with flowers) during a meeting of its Berlin state branch on 25 September 2026. Photograph: Tobias Schwarz/AFP/Getty Images Opinion Germany A leftwing victory in Berlin shows people want freedom, and liberals cannot deliver it Eva von Redecker Die Linke’s surge was propelled by a compelling promise: for voters to have the freedom to stay in their city. This is how to fight back against the far right Tue 29 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 03.26 EDT Share T he German leftwing party Die Linke won the state elections in Berlin on 20 September. It’s unclear whether the party will be able to form a coalition, appoint its lead candidate Elif Eralp as mayor , and follow through on her core campaign promise: to socialise the housing stock of the city’s biggest real-estate companies. A barrage of accusations started to circulate immediately after the results came in. Even by the standards of present-day polarisation, the pitch was extreme. On the basis of one leaked chat and one rapper’s performance , the party was described as schmoozing with criminal clans and endangering the lives of Berlin Jews . Accusations of antisemitism prompted the Greens and the SPD – potential coalition partners – to question any potential cooperation, while “alt-right” opinion-makers suggested that “Hamas and Hezbollah” had won the elections , or that the German Democratic Republic (the old East Germany) was about to come back. Alice Weidel of the rightwing AfD alleged that Die Linke intended to “shoot the rich”. Our liberal capitalist orders are designed to protect property. Touch one bit of it, and the whole thing is apparently on fire. And yet, nerves aren’t always this raw. The current flare-ups reveal a deep crisis. Sober-sounding commentators have pointed out that the accusations against Die Linke are simply a strategy to stop the socialisation agenda. But that account of moral panic as deliberate strategy can hardly explain everything. Why do so many people want to believe the smear campaigns, especially while the simultaneous wins for the AfD are swiftly normalised? The frenzy becomes less surprising once we understand the way in which liberalism is under pressure, and how that pressure predisposes the saner political forces to look like freedom’s foes. Freedom is the core of liberalism. It is freedom of a particular kind: individual freedom. It lets you do whatever you want as long as you don’t violate the freedom of others or, crucially, their property. The analogy between freedom and property runs deep: my entitlement to do whatever I want is derived from ownership of the self. I am my own quasi-property, and in that capacity I face other self-owners and rely on the state to adjudicate between us. This balance, between personal freedom and the freedom of all others, is already precarious , but in the face of the global crises we face now, it is especially under strain. Liberalism cannot govern economic inequality or ecological disaster, except by pitting the individual freedom of future or far-away others against the freedom of the currently privileged. Without democratic pride in our collective ability to rule our shared fate, the resulting policies look like sacrifice with no upside – I lose the (however hypothetical) freedom to own a row of houses, or I lose the freedom to drive a car, but even if I got public housing or public transport in turn, that wouldn’t register as compensation. After all, I cannot do whatever I want with those. View image in fullscreen The “time for a change” demonstration in Berlin, 12 September 2026, in which more than 100 organisations took part. Photograph: snapshot-photography/F Boillot/Shutterstock Reason might be on the side of anti-discrimination, social distancing or electric vehicles, but freedom kicks on the other side. It isn’t full liberal freedom any more, which would have to regard other people as a limit, but its unhinged, ultra-possessive part. The right offers quasi-property (or “phantom possession”, as I like to call it) to satisfy its voters: it defends traditional gender roles, the family, freedom of speech and the nation as though they were things to own. “Take back your country” was a core campaign slogan of the AfD. It alludes to the “great replacement” myth, according to which white populations are in the process of being replaced by people who are not. This plot weaves together several possessive entitlements: white citizens should “own” their country; the country and its men should “own” female reproductive powers to increase the domestic birthrate. And migrants aren’t even seen as capable of moving by their own will, but are imported by a woke or Jewish cabal, and now need to be removed by “remigration”. While such racist discourse is more associated with rural areas, “phantom possession” can suddenly override concern for fellow migrant citizens in Berlin, too. Any wrong step by the Left will suffice for the political middle to succumb to its own generalised property panic. Shaken by the success of the AfD, disoriented by a future that liberalism effectively cannot rule, challenged by emancipatory claims of various groups, and struggling to defend Israel’s crimes, much of the so-called centre also breaks the liberal pact that is founded on equality. In what some German Jews describe as “ paternalistic philosemitism ”, centrist pundits exceed the concern to fight antisemitism where it happens. Instead, they prop up an idea of absolute victimisation and defend it at all costs. They defend German “memory culture” as if it were their private asset. Consequently, Die Linke – just as human rights organisations, anti-zionist Jews, pro-Palestinian demonstrators and anyone perceived as vaguely “Arab” – is cast in the role of ruthless plunderer. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Berlin’s new political star is offering something all of Europe needs – hope and housing | Fatma Aydemir Read more How Die Linke – and its promise to socialise some private housing – will weather this particular campaign is still unknown. But whatever happens, it has to continue to navigate a fractured political map. Like all emancipatory efforts at present, its potential Berlin mayoralty is up against unhinged claims, and faces objective problems that require real change. Which is why the left cannot win within the liberal script. It can only win with a compelling formulation of freedom that points beyond the current impasse. Like Zohran Mamdani in New York, Die Linke has understood this. It has not only promised an abstract right, but literally the freedom to stay in one’s city, one’s neighbourhood, one’s flat. And this freedom can scale up: against displacement, genocide and the ecological doom that threatens our ability to remain on planet Earth. The German left urgently needs to find a way to translate such an agenda to the countryside, where parts of the white population have fallen for fascist myths. Which non-toxic freedom could repair their lost sense of place? And above all, how can we guarantee the freedom to stay for the migrant communities who are threatened with deportation by the AfD? Where this fails, even the most basic liberal achievement of human rights is lost. And definitely not because of socialised housing. Eva von Redecker is a philosopher and nonfiction writer. She is the author of The Freedom to Stay Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text: ‘In this environment of geopolitical tension, it feels like an incredible vulnerability’ … undersea security expert Elisabeth Braw. Photograph: Greg Funnell/The Guardian View image in fullscreen ‘In this environment of geopolitical tension, it feels like an incredible vulnerability’ … undersea security expert Elisabeth Braw. Photograph: Greg Funnell/The Guardian The ideas interview Books Interview Inside the undersea kingdom: the secret, sinister battle to control what lies beneath the waves Aida Edemariam Every day, trillions of dollars, oil and gas and 99% of the world’s web traffic move through undersea pipelines that bear no state’s protection. With superpowers and corporations vying for control, should we be worried about this new wild west? Thu 1 Oct 2026 07.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google O n Christmas Day 2024, six weeks before Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were due to disconnect themselves from Russia’s power grid, a Finnish engineer was just about to sit down to lunch when his phone rang. He was responsible for the Finnish side of the undersea cables that keep Finland and the Baltic states supplied with electricity, and one was malfunctioning. Within a couple of hours, authorities knew that a Cook Islands-registered tanker called the Eagle S, part of the shadow fleet carrying sanctioned Russian oil, in this case to Egypt, had sailed over the cable at the moment and location at which it had stopped working. The coastguard hailed the Eagle S. Were their anchors up? Yes, they replied – though they did not seem to check – and sailed on. Three hours later the ship hit another four cables in quick succession, nearly hobbling internet provision in Finland and Estonia – and was minutes away from a major electricity cable and the Balticconnector, which supplies the two countries with gas. Finland scrambled the border guard, which pulled up alongside the tanker and demanded the crew take up its anchor. But the Eagle S was not in Finnish territorial waters: the authorities could not force the captain to comply, and they did not know who or what might come to his aid. View image in fullscreen ‘It makes no sense’ … Seized oil tanker Eagle S in Porvoo, Finland. Photograph: Jussi Nukari/Rex/Shutterstock “It makes no sense,” says Swedish security expert Elisabeth Braw, leaning over a table in a well-upholstered corner of a private members’ club steps away from the Bank of England. She has spent the last couple of years talking to undersea engineers and coastguards about this and other similar incidents, rootling through accident investigation documents and court transcripts and Zoom-calling the small, specialised crews who have to go out and repair the damaged cables, often under extremely challenging conditions, asking them to show her what they are doing out there at sea. Now she has written it all up into a book bristling with enough incident to supply several action movies. “It makes no sense that you would drag your anchor across five cables, dozens of kilometres. No trained seafarer would do that. And they can say, ‘Well, I had no idea. We didn’t notice a thing.’ And how can you prove that that’s not the case?” The Undersea War paints an extraordinary picture of the bottom of the ocean, of fish and plant life threading through shipwrecks and junk thrown overboard – and especially of the “undersea spaghetti bowl” made of miles and miles of gas and oil pipes and electricity, telegraph and fibreoptic cables, the longest of which is 45,000km long and some of which are so delicate “even an inquisitive fish could damage them”. Vast amounts of electricity and oil, 95-99% of global internet traffic and $10tn (£7.75tn) of financial transactions travel through this system every day. “We assume the cloud is in the sky,” Braw writes, “but it’s underwater.” It is a system both incredibly fragile – take out a few cables off the coast of New York and New Jersey, and “Wall Street could become kneecapped in very short order”, as a Republican senator told her – and a source of great power, not least to anyone inclined to sabotage. View image in fullscreen ‘We assume the cloud is in the sky, but it’s under water’ … Elisabeth Braw. Photograph: Greg Funnell/The Guardian Braw, who has a direct, unfussy confidence and a dry sense of humour, began as a journalist before retraining in national security and specifically in so-called “grey zone” or sub-threshold threats (disinformation, election interference, cyber-attacks, cable sabotage). A government adviser (she won’t say which governments, only that they’re in Nato), and senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, she traces her interest back to watching Polish lorries loitering with intent around a cold war airbase near her childhood home in southern Sweden. The first newspaper article she remembers – she had just learned to read – was about a Soviet submarine that ran aground off the nearby city of Karlskrona in 1981, “the Soviet captain standing on top of the submarine” – she raises her arms as if in surrender. What if Trump got mad at Spain, which he often does, and told Google to disconnect it? A couple of years ago she was called as an expert witness to a House of Commons Defence Committee inquiry into grey-zone threats and was struck that while the parliamentarians were serious, and knowledgable about the subject, they were “taken aback by the realisation that it’s very hard to protect undersea infrastructure. It’s not like you can say, ‘Oh, well, here’s what we should do. It’s expensive, but it’s going to happen.’ That solution doesn’t exist.” The thing that still amazes her is that “behind every email, credit card payment, and Zoom call is an ocean worker” – and just how few of them there are. Talking to Braw, it’s impossible not to be struck by how oblivious most people are to what she calls the “undersea kingdom”. “Well, it’s out of sight, out of mind, right? And undersea cables and pipelines are really out of sight.” Even the most sophisticated organisations in the world seem to have based everything on blind trust that everything will be OK, that everyone will behave. “We don’t have a global government and the entire structure is based on countries committing to doing something and then following through, abiding by the rules they’ve agreed to follow” – ie the 1994 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos). “We don’t have a higher authority that can force them to follow the rules. And it’s extraordinary that it has worked so well, that we’ve been able to build the entire modern economy on that assumption.” View image in fullscreen ‘New order of impunity’ … French President Emmanuel Macron addresses the UN in New York earlier this month. Photograph: Kyle Mazza/CNP/Kyle Mazza - CNP/Shutterstock All that trust is quite touching, really. Except, increasingly, powerful people and states are seemingly choosing what Emmanuel Macron, addressing the UN in New York last week, called “ the new order of impunity ”. In an ideal world, or even the world of 15 years ago, you might say, “Well, we are going to set up a global flotilla led by the United States, with Russia, China, Germany, the UK, France, to make sure these pirates, whoever they are, who are harming cables, don’t do it,” says Braw. But that, clearly, is a pipe dream, one that is now further complicated by big tech laying its own cables. “Since the very first cable [in 1858] it has been, you know, one road for everybody. We’ve all travelled, our traffic has travelled, on those communal roads.” But now Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon are planning about 60 of their own; Meta’s Waterworth cable will be the longest ever, at 50,000km, and wrap around the world. There was an interesting moment in the parliamentary hearing, says Braw, when Mike Martin MP worried about the “absolute insanity that a key piece of critical national infrastructure is going to be delivered and owned by tech giants, over which we have no control”. Ireland is the original cable junction. It has bet the house on globalisation and peace … it’s so exposed “On one hand, it’s business,” Braw says now. “If they can create these cables, then more power to them. On the other hand, in this environment of geopolitical tension, it does feel like an incredible potential vulnerability. What if Trump got mad at Spain, which he often does, and told Google to disconnect Spain? Because Google has this super-duper cable between Spain and the US East Coast. Or what if Google thought that the way to please Trump on some other matter would be to suspend traffic?” There has already, she writes, been a kind of precedent, when in 2023 Elon Musk momentarily blocked Starlink access to Crimea . Then there are all the pinch points : off the east coast of the US, for instance, off Japan, off Ireland. About 75% of transatlantic cable traffic goes through Irish waters , in which Russian vessels have recently been seen lurking – while the Irish navy is tiny. “They are so defenceless,” says Braw. “Ireland is the original cable junction and it’s still a cable junction because of its location. It has bet the house on globalisation, and peace” – and headquartering big tech. “And now that can no longer be taken for granted, Ireland is so exposed.” What if something happened? They’d probably have to turn to the Royal Navy, Braw replies, bluntly. Which would “obviously be hugely humiliating”. Iran has recently opened a whole new front by suggesting it might impose tolls on cables traversing the strait of Hormuz. And underneath all this is the question of what, exactly, constitutes an act of war. Because defining what is going on is the first step in working out how to respond. Suppose, Braw says, that a cable company reports an issue. Then the coastguard sails out to the approximate site. They might identify a suspect, but then they have to decide, while that is happening, whether it’s just an accident, or “whether it’s the first step towards something much bigger” – which would involve the navy, and thus a military response, and who knows what after that. In the case of the Eagle S, Finnish authorities ordered the boat in towards their coast and abseiled on to it – knowing, all the while, that as it was carrying Russian oil, they could be setting something far bigger in motion. (Thankfully, this did not happen. The crew were arrested and although eventually found guilty of criminal damage, Finnish law could not be applied and no sentence enforced because the incident had happened outside their territorial waters.) And in fact, the interception, some months later, of a tanker called the Jaguar, which was sailing under no flag at all, prompted a Russian fighter jet to enter Estonian airspace . There has been, in recent weeks, an increase in chatter about a possible imminent attack by Russia on European soil. Braw largely dismisses this – not least because she can’t see why Russia, already overstretched in Ukraine, would do something so expensive when all it takes is an errant anchor and plausible deniability. And “if you engage in sabotage, disinformation, election interference, arson, using drones, then what is the target country supposed to do?” There is a kind of very dark humour in the fact that the only people properly intent on defining what exactly counts as war at the moment seem to be “insurers, the companies they insure – and district judges. It is extraordinary.” View image in fullscreen Sea change … TransPacific communication cables on the ocean floor off the island of Guam, Micronesia. Photograph: David Fleetham/Alamy There is another type of sabotage to contend with, too. It has been known for decades that the ocean contains treasure – specifically, potato-shaped nodules containing elements such as manganese, iron, aluminium, nickel, copper, cobalt, potassium, titanium, barium and rare earths – that can, in theory, simply be picked off the ocean floor. Some of them, the larger ones, have been there for up to 15m years. Especially attractive are the nodules in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, an abyssal (deep and flat) plain between Hawaii and Mexico in the Pacific, which contains vast amounts of minerals, and over which no country has jurisdiction. But when the Law of the Sea came into force in 1994, the International Seabed Authority was also created: any mining has to be agreed to by all members (170 countries plus the EU). The US never ratified the law of the sea, but this has until recently been largely a technicality, because the American navy has sailed the world enforcing it, and the US government, understanding the importance of the ISA, has attended its meetings. Thirty-one licences for exploration have been issued, but no one has mined – in fact, a bloc of 40 countries, including the UK, think there should be a moratorium on any commercial mining, not least because it is such a complex and fragile ecosystem, poorly understood, and no one has any idea what damage would be done. (A position underlined when, earlier this year, scientists announced the discovery of a whole new family of crustacean species in the Clarion-Clipperton.) But last April Donald Trump signed an executive order allowing mining in international waters , including outside US jurisdiction. Five days later they received their first application , a request to mine the Clarion-Clipperton zone. Braw believes the main impetus is the Trump administration’s wish to reduce their dependence on China, especially for the rare earths used in digital devices . The trouble is, “processing will still have to happen in China unless America wants to set up processing plants, and it’s very dirty, which is why China specialises in it. Nobody wants to have processing plants in their community, in their backyard.” View image in fullscreen ‘The undersea kingdom has everything’ … sunset over the Baltic Sea. Photograph: Jorg Greuel/Getty Images An even larger risk is the precedent it sets. “The thing about America launching unilateral deep-sea mining is that China can say, ‘Since this arrangement clearly doesn’t work, we’ll start mining unilaterally as well.’ And how do you then figure out who gets what? It’s completely outside an international legal framework. It’s the wild west. You can have two companies backed by two different countries fighting for the same pile of nodules.” Or, as Braw puts it in her book: “A battle for commercial domination of the undersea realm could turn into a surface war between the world’s most powerful fleets.” Instead, she argues, we could just recycle our tech and aim to use no new rare earths at all: “That’s what the European Union is focusing on.” “The undersea kingdom has everything,” says Braw. “It is such a combination of mystery and hi-tech. And the hi-tech that sits there, it functions, it works well, it doesn’t harm anybody. But I think if we start messing with this undersea kingdom, either for hostile purposes or for selfish reasons, then we risk upsetting it, and it’s to the detriment of the maritime environment but also to the detriment of our modern life, because the balance is so delicate.” Surely we can stop this happening? With deep-sea mining specifically, says Braw, you would need to “plead with the next US president to reverse the executive order, since it’s based on an executive order, not legislation”. And is the international law simply no longer fit for purpose? Given that the US cannot be trusted, what should happen next? “Well, the first thing that needs to happen is the world needs to realise who the heroes are. It’s the cable crews that go out defying the elements, but now also having to worry that when they go to cable repair sites they themselves could become some sort of target.” As for the larger picture, the sea has been called the “blue commons” ; it belongs to all of us, and we need, Braw argues, “the countries of the world that believe in maritime order to get together and show that we are the majority. Eight politicians who belong to the United for Ukraine Parliamentary Network are meeting with Canadian decision-makers. Justin Tang/The Canadian Press Comments Share Save for later Please log in to bookmark this story. Log In Create Free Account A delegation of European lawmakers is in Ottawa this week urging Canada to mount a more forceful response to Russia’s continuing war on Ukraine, including pressing China into ending its support for Moscow in the conflict. Ivanna Klympush-Tsintsadze, a member of the Ukrainian Parliament, was among a group of eight politicians who belong to the United for Ukraine Parliamentary Network and are meeting with Canadian decision-makers. She said Canada has been exemplary in applying sanctions along with other Western allies against Russians and others responsible for Moscow’s assault on Ukraine. Ms. Klympush-Tsintsadze said Canada should more directly help Europeans in “cutting the Russian ability to carry on this war effort” by finding ways to ship natural gas and oil to the continent and supplant Moscow’s energy sales to Europe. She remarked on Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to strengthen ties with Chinese President Xi Jinping, saying Ottawa should speak up for Ukraine when talking to Beijing. As Group of Seven foreign ministers noted in a joint statement last November, China remains a “decisive enabler” of Russia’s war on Ukraine. Beijing flouts Western sanctions to buy Moscow’s petroleum, to supply parts for weapons and, through some smaller banks and money-transfer systems, provide financial services to Russians. “We see that your leadership is also seeking contacts with China,” the Ukrainian MP said. “China is the country that is backing the Russian military effort. So maybe use your contacts with China to that extent,” she said. Ukraine discloses evidence of its military operations against Russia in Africa Ms. Klympush-Tsintsadze suggested pressure from other countries could give Beijing pause. “Maybe they care about some remnants of their reputation, and try to stop that assistance,” she said of China. “So there are ways, I think, where Canada could be, with its stance, much more results oriented.” Canada has committed more than $26-billion in support, both civilian and military, to Ukraine since 2022. Oleksandr Merezhko, another member of Ukraine’s Parliament, said his country is not just fighting Russia but a coalition of countries backing Moscow including Iran, North Korea, Cuba and China. “Without Chinese support, without Chinese money, Russia would have to stop the war,” he said, adding possibly one of the biggest geopolitical shifts taking place these days is cash-strapped Russia’s increasing dependence on Beijing. “Russia is turning into the vassal of China,” he said. The group has been meeting with Canadian members of Parliament, senators and think tanks and plans to meet Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Thursday, among others. Open this photo in gallery: Oleksandr Merezhko, shown in Kyiv in 2025, said his country is not just fighting Russia but a coalition of countries that backs Moscow. Olga Ivashchenko/The Globe and Mail Russia’s all-out assault on Ukraine began in February, 2022, and several of the visiting Europeans remarked on how little coverage they see in Canadian media of the conflict. Mr. Merezkho warned that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s appetite for territory will not stop at Ukraine. He predicted that Moscow will eventually invade neighbouring Moldova to seize its Transnistria region. “It’s a war for Russian-speaking people. And each country which has Russian-speaking minorities is in danger,” the MP said. The politicians, also from Lithuania, Poland, Estonia, Finland and Latvia, said Canadians must wake up to the fact that Russia is testing NATO every day. “He is a provocateur. He makes a provocation, and he sees what happens. If there is no strong reaction, he moves further,” Mr. Merezkho said of Mr. Putin. Some European leaders and military brass have said that Russia by 2029 will have the capacity to attack another North Atlantic Treaty Organization country. Zelensky warns Russia of consequences if energy truce talks fail Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned last week, citing unnamed intelligence agencies, that Russia plans to launch “hybrid” drone and ​missile attacks against countries supporting Ukraine. Agnieszka Pomaska, a Polish lawmaker, said Russia is testing NATO every day, citing sabotage on railways, GPS jamming, drones or incursions into alliance airspace. “It’s not about 2029,” she said. “It’s about the next year.” She noted that a Russian military helicopter Wednesday briefly entered Polish airspace. “Every day on my phone in the morning, I receive any information that there was some kind of alarm at the border, close to the border, or even in my city or somewhere in the continent,” Ms. Pomaska said. Rihards Kols, a Latvian member of the European Parliament, said he believes Mr. Putin’s “dream is to test Article Five” of NATO, the collective-defence clause that obliges members to consider an attack against any to be an attack against all. Russia is trying to find ways to attack alliance members that will not trigger a collective response, he said. Trump administration invites Putin to December G20 meeting, possible summit Mr. Kols said it’s unfortunate that European leaders describe Russian hostile actions – computer hacking or sabotage – as “hybrid” attacks because it “tones down the seriousness” of these actions. Hybrid is an adjective used to describe measures that are below the threshold of conventional armed conflict. He believes Mr. Putin will not be satisfied with a ceasefire in Ukraine if one arises – and will want to deploy his battle-hardened troops elsewhere after. “The Russia threat will not just fade away,” Mr. Kols predicted. “It’s just matter of time when the resources will be mobilized to push and penetrate somewhere else.” With reports from Reuters Report an editorial error Report a technical issue Editorial code of conduct Related stories Russian strikes kill eight in Ukraine after Zelensky appeals for Russia sanctions at UN Russia bombards Kyiv with drones as Zelensky addresses UN Russia targets Zaporizhzhia after Ukraine’s 1,000-drone weekend barrage Russian strikes kill eight in Ukraine after Zelensky appeals for Russia sanctions at UN Russia bombards Kyiv with drones as Zelensky addresses UN Russia targets Zaporizhzhia after Ukraine’s 1,000-drone weekend barrage Diversions Horoscope Daily astrology with Sally Brompton Daily Crossword Solve today's puzzle Daily Cryptic Witty word play at its best Sudoku Three difficulty levels to solve Follow related authors and topics Steven Chase Follow You must be logged in to follow. Home Paid news feed Foto Agerpres Press Monitoring Bucharest Phone: +4 021.2076.110 Mirabela Gradinaru: Coming years' challenge - turning creative energy into strategic advantage for Romania Category: English Date: 2026-10-06 00:55:16 Foto: Silviu MATEI / AGERPRES Photo The problem is not that Romania lacks creativity; the challenge is to identify it, connect it and create the space it needs to develop, Mirabela Gradinaru, partner of President Nicusor Dan, said on Monday at the roundtable debate 'Creative Romania: Observatory & Laboratory of Creative Ecologies,' held as part of the second edition of Romanian Creative Week X Bucharest and hosted by the 'Carol I' Central University Library. 'What is happening here is more than a conversation about the creative industries. It is a conversation about collaboration, about bridges between fields and about our ability to build together. Ultimately, this is what it comes down to: how do we build together for Romania? The most valuable ideas often emerge at the intersection of different perspectives. And that is exactly what you are doing here today, bringing together multiple fields and different viewpoints. We know Romania has a deep connection to its heritage and traditions, but it also has people working at the forefront of technology and innovation. We do not have to choose between the past and the future. Our challenge is to discover what we can build when we come together. And when we talk about creative ecologies, we are really talking about ecosystems of trust and collaboration. Creativity does not flourish in isolation. It needs connections, people who share ideas, institutions that support such initiatives, and I hope that the presence of the Presidential Administration here today underscores its desire to support all creative industries, as well as communities that encourage experimentation and the courage to try something new. Because very often what we lack is courage, even when initiatives do exist,' Mirabela Gradinaru said. She noted that in the past, 'a nation's strength was measured primarily by the resources it possessed.' 'Today, in an economy based on knowledge and innovation, I am convinced that our competitive advantage increasingly lies in our ability to generate ideas and turn them into solutions that are relevant to society, helping address the various challenges societies face today,' she opined. 'Creative industries do not merely produce cultural goods, products or services; they create opportunities. They create the opportunity for a city to reinvent itself, for a community to make its voice heard, and for a young person to build a future here in Romania. And I sincerely believe that the challenge of the coming years is to transform the creative energy we possess into a strategic advantage for the country's development, especially in the era of AI. The future belongs not only to those who have resources, but to those who have the imagination, courage and ability to turn ideas into reality,' Gradinaru stressed. The roundtable discussion 'Creative Romania: Observatory & Laboratory of Creative Ecologies,' hosted by Marlene Herberth, focused on how Romanian creativity can be recognised, connected and supported over the long term. 'Romania needs to become better at recognising, connecting and supporting the creativity it already has. Through my work at the intersection of heritage, contemporary art and communities, I see how much the continuity of an idea depends on the relationships that sustain it: who passes on knowledge, who provides space for experimentation, who finances projects and who opens access to the public,' the host of the event said. Presidential advisor Valentin-Sorin Costreie said one of Romania's challenges is related to creativity. 'The invitation was for a roundtable that does not physically exist, but we are using our imagination and here we have a roundtable, in fact several small round tables. And I was thinking that this is Romania's problem as well. Romania already has islands of creativity that have been recognised and that already export creative output. The challenge is how we bring these small round tables together into one large roundtable called Creative Romania. I don't believe this can be achieved unless we start from the ground up, from a very early stage, I would say beginning with early childhood education in kindergarten and the first years of school, and cultivate something we have not really nurtured. (...) Why should we have a Creative Romania? Our educational system is neither designed nor tailored to foster creativity. Quite the opposite. (...) What should we do to become more creative? We need to change the educational paradigm across society. We need to nurture the curiosity that we naturally possess. Children are highly creative and inventive. The problem is that we place them into rigid frameworks, and in doing so we lose much of their creative potential,' he argued. Costreie stressed that Romania has 'potential which, when nurtured through the commitment of mentors, parents and role models these children should have, can thrive.' 'I believe we need to nurture their creativity and provide them with role models,' he added. Participants in the 'Creative Romania: Observatory & Laboratory of Creative Ecologies' roundtable meeting included architect Teodor Frolu, founding member of the Bucharest Urban Space Association; visual artist Andrei Cozlac - curator of RCW's New Media District; Andrei Boncea - president of the Film Producers Alliance; designer Ioana Ciolacu, president of the Romanian Fashion Council; Anca Lupes - president of RAW Music and founder of Mastering The Music Business; and Bogdan Trambaciu - director of the Project Management Unit within the Ministry of Culture. Romanian Creative Week X Bucharest runs through October 8, bringing contemporary art, fashion, installations and events dedicated to the creative industries to the capital.
